title: In a meeting
why: This lesson closes the work unit with the meeting: taking the floor, proposing, agreeing or disagreeing with tact, and concluding. You reuse the conditional and the connectors you know, and you learn the vocabulary of projects, including the false friend délai.

Opening the meeting and taking the floor

French meetings (les réunions) can be lively: people interrupt, add comments, come back to an earlier point. To take part, you need a few formulas to start, to take the floor and to add an idea without sounding rude.

FrenchEnglish
Bon, on commence ?Right, shall we start?
Le premier point à l'ordre du jour, c'est le budget.The first item on the agenda is the budget.
On fait le point sur le projet.Let's review where we are on the project.
Si je peux me permettre…If I may…
Je peux dire un mot ?Can I say something?
Je voudrais ajouter que…I'd like to add that…
Pardon de vous interrompre, mais…Sorry to interrupt, but…
Pour revenir au budget…To come back to the budget…

L'ordre du jour is the agenda of a meeting (your personal planner is un agenda: careful!). Faire le point means to take stock, to review where things stand: On fait le point lundi ? is one of the most frequent sentences in a French office.

Si je peux me permettre, je voudrais ajouter que le client est très content.If I may, I'd like to add that the client is very happy.

Si je peux me permettre is the polite door-opener, a cousin of je me permets de vous écrire from the email lesson. In a meeting it softens anything that follows, even a disagreement.

", "

Proposing, agreeing, disagreeing

To make a proposal, French has several options, from the most direct to the softest.

FrenchEnglish
Je propose de reporter la réunion.I suggest postponing the meeting.
On pourrait demander l'avis du client.We could ask the client's opinion.
Il faudrait finir avant vendredi.We ought to finish before Friday.
Et si on faisait une pause ?How about taking a break?

After je propose de, use an infinitive: English “I suggest postponing” becomes je propose de reporter (not an -ing form). Et si on faisait… ? is the fixed formula you met for invitations: si + imparfait = “how about…?”. The conditional (on pourrait, il faudrait, nous devrions) makes everything more diplomatic.

Reacting

agreeingdisagreeing (politely)
Je suis tout à fait d'accord.Je ne suis pas d'accord.
Bonne idée !Je ne suis pas tout à fait d'accord.
Exactement.Je comprends, mais…
Je suis d'accord avec Léa.Je ne suis pas sûr / sûre.

Être d'accord means “to agree”: never say “je suis agréé” or “j'agrée”. Tout à fait (completely) strengthens it; pas tout à fait (not entirely) is the classic French way to disagree softly.

In speech, par contre (on the other hand, however) is everywhere in meetings: L'idée est bonne. Par contre, le délai est court.

", "

Concluding and following up

At the end of a meeting, someone sums up, opens the floor for questions and asks who will write the report.

FrenchEnglish
Pour résumer…To sum up…
En conclusion…In conclusion…
Avez-vous des questions ?Do you have any questions?
Qui fait le compte rendu ?Who's taking the minutes?
Je m'en occupe.I'll take care of it.
On se retrouve mardi pour faire le point.We'll meet again on Tuesday to review.

Words of the project

Le projet, la date limite (the deadline), le délai and le compte rendu (the minutes, the report). Watch the false friend: le délai is the time allowed to do something (un délai de deux semaines, le délai est court), not a delay. A delay, being late, is un retard.

Le délai est court : la date limite, c'est le 15 mars.The timeline is tight: the deadline is March 15.

On or nous?

In the meeting itself, people say on: On commence ? On fait le point. In the written minutes, you switch to nous: Nous gardons la date du 15 mars. The verb changes too: on garde but nous gardons.

The French love to end a meeting by scheduling the next one. If you volunteer for the minutes, say Je m'en occupe, then Je vous l'envoie cet après-midi: you'll sound perfectly at ease.
